1:
Keil sets out the chapter's three heads before anything else: the priests were not to defile themselves by touching the dead or by signs of mourning, they were to contract and maintain a spotless marriage, and those with bodily failings were to keep away from the duties of the office. Ellicott stops on the way they are addressed. The phrase the priests the sons of Aaron occurs only here, every other place in the Pentateuch having it the other way about, and he takes the inversion to be deliberate — they are priests by virtue of being Aaron's sons and not from any merit of their own, and are to impress the same on their children, whom the second Temple authorities read the phrase as obliging them to bring up fit for the hereditary office. Calvin explains why so much weight rests on small things. The priests were to differ from the rest of the people by notable marks, since special purity became those who represented the person of Christ; the legal rites were steps by which Israel might ascend to the study of true holiness, and though bodily exercise profiteth little, the use of the ancient shadows must be estimated by their end.

What counted as defilement the text does not say, and Ellicott notes that it was left to the administrators of the Law to define — who enacted that not only touching a dead body but coming within four cubits of it, entering the house where it lay, entering a burial place, following to the grave, or showing mourning at all, pollutes the priest and unfits him for the sanctuary. Henry gives the same tradition in English measure, that it made a man unclean to come within six feet of a corpse, and adds the consequence: since all who entered the tent where a body lay were unclean seven days, every mourner at a funeral defiled himself for a week. Clarke states it plainest: no priest was to assist in laying out a dead body or preparing it for burial. Ellicott's best note is on the exception. Where the corpse is among people whose business it is to bury it, the priest is forbidden to take part; but where a priest, or even the high priest, finds a body on the road and can call no one to bury it, he is obliged to perform that last office himself — and knowing how much the ancient Hebrews thought of burial, and that nothing horrified them like an unburied body, one appreciates the humanity of the provision.

On the mourning itself Henry finds the law generous before it is severe. God put an honour upon natural affection by dispensing with his servants' attendance for seven days while they indulged their sorrow for a near relation; but beyond that, weeping must not hinder sowing. He turns it into a charge to ministers: they must be examples of patience under affliction, and particularly under the affliction that touches in the tenderest part, since they know better than most why we must not sorrow as those who have no hope, and ought to be eminently calm and composed, that they may comfort others with the same comforts wherewith they are themselves comforted of God. Calvin concedes how hard that is — a rare virtue, so to repress our feelings when deprived of brothers or friends that the bitterness of grief does not overcome our composure — and gives the restraint a positive meaning, that abstinence from mourning manifests the hope of the blessed resurrection, the priests being forbidden to mourn precisely so that the people might seek consolation from them. The figure was fulfilled in Christ, who bore not grief only but the extreme horror of death, yet was free from every stain and gloriously triumphed, so that the very recollection of his cross wipes away our tears.
2:
The exceptions are seven, and the first of them is not named. Ellicott reports that the administrators of the Law took the phrase his flesh that is near unto him to mean his wife, the Chaldee of Jonathan rendering it so outright; Gill argues the same from the Hebrew, that the words mean the other part of himself, one flesh with him, and adds Jarchi's dictum that there is no flesh of his but his wife — if she is not intended here she is nowhere expressed, and Ezekiel being specially forbidden to mourn for his wife shows that the permission was ordinary. Wesley agrees and gives the reason: these exceptions God makes in condescension to human infirmity, because in such cases it was very hard to restrain the affections, though the allowance concerns the inferior priest and not the high priest. Ellicott notices something else in the list. This is one of only three places in the Bible where the mother is named before the father, and the Jewish canonists explain it by saying that a son's fitness for the priesthood depends more on his having a good mother — the rules about whom a priest might marry being so stringent that the slightest infringement disqualified the son, and when a city was besieged and taken all the priests' wives had to be divorced for fear they had suffered violence.

The maiden sister is defined by where she lives rather than how she is related. Gill canvasses whether she is a sister by both parents or by one, and suspects the qualifying phrase marks nearness of place, since being unmarried she remained in her father's house until she died; Wesley says the same, that the nearness meant is of habitation, one not yet cut off from the family; and Ellicott explains what changes at marriage — she goes to her husband, ceases to be near her brother, and it devolves on the husband to attend the funeral rites. He adds a point that reverses the tenor of the law: for these seven relations the priest was not merely permitted to contract defilement but obliged to. Then the disputed clause. Clarke notes that the word rendered chief man may equally mean master or husband, and lists the two readings — that as a chief it would be improper to see him in the humiliation mourning implies, or that though a husband he must not defile himself even for a wife because the anointing of his God is upon him — preferring the first. Ellicott takes the second and pushes it further, reading the verse as restricting the permission to a lawfully married wife, so that a priest who had contracted a profaning marriage could not attend her funeral at all; he calls this the reading that does least violence to a manifestly disordered text.

The mourning customs forbidden next are all heathen, and each commentator supplies an instance. Gill traces the shaving to the Chaldeans and the Greeks, noting that when Hephestion died Alexander shaved his soldiers and himself in imitation of Achilles, and that the priests of Isis were called by Minutius Felix her bald priests. Clarke reports from Herodotus that the Egyptian priests shaved the whole body every third day lest any uncleanness be about them when they ministered, and finds the same picture in Baruch, where the priests of Babylon sit with their clothes rent and their heads and beards shaven — from which he turns on his own century: everyone knows the tonsure of the Catholic priests, and should not that be avoided as an approach to a heathenish custom? Ellicott observes that the three practices were forbidden to the people at large as well, and that the ordinary Israelites indulged in them notwithstanding. Wesley gives the reason for binding the priests more strictly: they are by word and example to teach the people their duty.
7:
Two words govern the rule, and they are read differently. Gill takes a whore for a common prostitute and profane for a woman whose chastity has been violated, willingly or unwillingly, but who has not made a practice of it — while noting that the Jewish writers read both terms of descent rather than conduct, a whore meaning one not born of an Israelite and a profane one born of a forbidden marriage. Clarke defines them morally and adds a third: a prostitute, though even reclaimed; a heathen, or one not a cordial believer in the true God; and a divorced woman, because that very circumstance might raise the suspicion that the priest and she had been improperly connected before. Wesley extends the second word to a woman deflowered secretly or by force, on the principle that the priest must keep every member of his family free not only from gross wickedness but from all suspicion of evil. Ellicott marks the turn the chapter takes here: from defilement contracted through the dead the lawgiver passes to the priest's alliances with the living, which might carry still more serious consequences for his office, so that in choosing a wife he must be careful of both her chastity and her descent.

Calvin explains why so much is asked. The same cause holds now as then, since Paul directs that pastors be chosen who rule well their own houses, lest those appointed to govern the Church be despised for their domestic vices; but God had regard most especially to the priesthood of Christ, that it should not be exposed to contempt. He is careful about what is being forbidden: no law kept a private Israelite from marrying a divorced or a deflowered woman, and what was permitted to the multitude God condemned in the priests, to withdraw them from every mark of infamy — for if the people had not reverenced them, all religion would have been contemptible. The command to sanctify him is therefore addressed to the people. Keil takes it as more than respecting his dignity, which is Knobel's reading, and as charging the nation, in the persons of its chiefs, to see that he did not desecrate his office by a polluted marriage. Gill makes the magistrate the enforcer, quoting Jarchi's blunt gloss that he is to be sanctified whether he will or no, and beaten until he puts such a wife away. Ellicott draws out the other half of the arrangement: the priest is placed under the supervision of the people, but where he keeps the law they must reverence him, which is why he takes precedence at public assemblies, reads first from the Law in the synagogue, and says the blessing at table to this day.

The daughter's case is severer than her father's. Keil states the sentence plainly, that in profaning herself she profaned him, and was to be stoned and then burned. Gill takes up the question the rabbis raise, whether the law means a daughter betrothed or married — the Targum restricting it to the betrothed, Jarchi and Aben Ezra allowing either, and all agreeing that a wholly unattached daughter is not in view. Gill finds no such exception in the text, and offers a reason why the verse would otherwise be redundant: any man's betrothed daughter guilty of this was already to die, so a separate law for the priest's daughter would be needless — unless it was made solely for the sake of the different death, burning being the more terrible.
10:
Clarke marks the title as new: this is the first place the phrase occurs, and it is emphatic in the Hebrew — that priest, the great one — so that as a representative of our Lord he was required to be especially holy, and stands as God's king among the people. Gill passes on what the Jews required of that greatness: he was to exceed his brethren in beauty, in strength, in wisdom and in riches, and if his money fell short the other priests were to give him of theirs, each according to his wealth, until he was the richest of them all. Ellicott identifies the two marks of his consecration, the profuse pouring of oil that distinguished it from the ordinary priest's, and the robing, which he would render consecrated by putting on the garments rather than to put them on, since the vesting was itself part of the ceremony. Henry hears the phrase about the crown of the anointing oil as more than description: the anointing of the Spirit is, to all that have it, a crown of glory and a diadem of beauty.

The signs of grief forbidden him are the ordinary ones. Wesley notes that uncovering the head was then the posture of mourners, though the custom later changed and mourners covered them instead; and Ellicott would render the clause that he shall not let his head be dishevelled, adding from the Chaldee that the rending of clothes is forbidden in the time of distress. His reason for the prohibition is the best offered: sustaining that position and standing as intercessor between God and man, such outward expressions of sorrow might lead the people for whom he ministers to believe that he was impugning the justice of the divine judgment. Henry pushes it harder — he must show himself perfectly unconcerned in all the crosses and comforts of this life, his natural affection swallowed up in compassion for the ignorant and concern for the household of God he was made ruler of, so that the holy one entrusted with the thummim and urim must not know father or mother. Keil adds the limit that keeps the rule from becoming absurd: he was not to leave the sanctuary to give way to grief or attend a funeral, but we are not to understand from this, as Bähr and Baumgarten maintain, that the sanctuary was to be his constant abode.

On the dead body itself Ellicott records how far the later authorities extended it — any portion of a corpse counted, so that entering a place where a certain quantity of its blood lay defiled him, the literal phrase being any dead soul, and the soul being in the blood. He also states the contrast that defines the office: where the ordinary priest was obliged to attend the funerals of seven relations, the high priest was not permitted to join even his parents', the single exception being a body found in an isolated place, which it was meritorious in him to bury. Gill notices that the heathen afterwards imitated the rule, the Flamen Dialis at Rome being forbidden to go where a body was burnt or buried, and a branch of cypress being set at the door of a house of death so that a high priest should not enter unawares. Henry gives a practical reason for the stricter rule — an ordinary priest defiled could be replaced by another, whereas a defiled high priest left a greater want — and then turns it round: our Lord, the great high priest of our profession, touched the dead body of Jairus's daughter, the bier of the widow's son and the grave of Lazarus, to show that he came to alter the property of death and take off the terror of it, for now that it cannot destroy, it does not defile.
13:
Everything in the rule is narrowed. Gill takes a wife to mean one and not two, citing Ben Gersom and Maimonides for the view that though polygamy was practised by Israelites and even by ordinary priests, the high priest might never have two women together — and notes the parallel that the Egyptians, who took as many wives as they pleased, allowed their priests but one, as a minister of the New Testament is to be the husband of one wife. Ellicott sets out the four conclusions the second-Temple authorities drew from the verse: that the high priest must have one wife where ordinary priests might have several, that she must be a virgin under thirteen, that she must not even have been betrothed to another, and that she must be of Jewish parentage by race, where the ordinary priest might marry a proselyte's daughter — the first of which Paul enjoins on Christian bishops, and the last of which the Greek version actually spells out. Gill explains the age: the Talmudists required one whose puberty was not fully completed, so that there could be no doubt at all of her virginity. Clarke rests the question on the noun, which he takes as full proof that bethulah is the proper Hebrew word for a virgin, from a root meaning to separate, since such a person stood in her separate state and had never in any way been united to a man.

Calvin raises an objection nobody else does and answers it with unexpected humanity. Someone may object that the marriage of an old priest to a young girl is ridiculous and indecorous and liable to many inconveniences — to which he replies that special regulations must be so expounded as not to interfere with general principles. If a decrepit old man falls in love with a young girl it is a base and shameful lust; he will defraud her if he marries her; jealousy and wretched anxiety will follow; or else, by dotingly seeking to keep his wife's love, he will throw away all regard for gravity. God, in forbidding the high priest any but a virgin, did not mean to violate a rule dictated by nature and reason: allowance being made for age, he wanted modesty and propriety maintained in the marriage, so that an elderly priest should marry a virgin not too far from his own years — and where a man was failing and little fitted for marriage at all, the law that he must marry a virgin amounted rather to an exhortation to celibacy. Wesley gives the other reason for requiring a virgin, that as the high priest was a type of Christ, so his wife was a type of the church, which is compared to a virgin.

The widow is excluded on every construction. Gill and Ellicott agree that the ban covers the widow of a priest and of any Israelite alike, and reaches even a virgin who had been betrothed to a man who died before marrying her, since betrothal made her his widow; but both record the exception that if he had betrothed a widow before being raised to the pontificate he might marry her afterwards, Gill naming Joshua the son of Gamla as the instance. Gill adds the one duty the office cancelled: where another man was bound, when his brother died childless, to marry the widow, the high priest was to have his shoe plucked off instead. Keil closes the section on the reason given for all of it, that a marriage out of keeping with the holiness of his rank would profane not only himself but his posterity among his people.
16:
Keil states the principle behind the list: as the spiritual nature of a man is reflected in his bodily form, only a faultless condition of body could correspond to the holiness of the priest — and he notes that the Greeks and Romans required the same thing of their priests for the very same reason, citing Plato and Seneca and Plutarch. Ellicott marks the transition: having forbidden the priests to disfigure themselves or to disqualify their descendants by illegal marriages, the legislator turns to blemishes not voluntarily contracted at all, which disqualify as surely. Keil then works through the terms, most of them obscure — one mutilated, particularly about the face; one with any member beyond the normal size; the hunchback; one whose limb is unnaturally thin or withered rather than merely wasted; one spotted in the eye, which he takes for a white speck rather than the blear-eyed of the Greek; and two skin conditions he identifies from the versions as the itch and the ringworm.

Whether such a rule still binds is where the commentators part company, and neither is tentative. Clarke could hardly be more emphatic: never was a wiser, a more rational, and a more expedient law enacted relative to sacred matters, since a man who ministers in holy things should have nothing in his person or manner that cannot render him respectable to those he serves, and any personal defect that makes him contemptible will greatly injure his usefulness if it does not prevent it entirely. Let no man say this is part of the Mosaic law and we are not bound by it — it is an eternal law, founded on reason, propriety, common sense and absolute necessity. He allows one exception, that scars received in the work of God, by persecution or otherwise, are honourable and add to a man's respectability. Henry says the reverse in as many words. Under the gospel those who labour under such blemishes have reason to thank God that they are not thereby shut out from offering spiritual sacrifices, nor, if otherwise qualified, from the ministry itself — for there is many a healthful beautiful soul lodged in a crazy deformed body. What he does infer is a different disqualification: those whose minds are blemished by a reigning vice are unfit, being spiritually blind and lame and crooked, and the deformities of Hophni and Phinehas were worse than any named here.

Henry gives the reason the Law itself had, that great men choose sightly servants, and that comely men were especially required for the people's sake, who judge by outward appearance and would think meanly of a service performed by someone despicable to look at — the provision being made to keep the altar from falling into contempt. But he is careful about what was not withdrawn: the blemished priest still ate of the sacrifices, even the most holy things, since the blemishes were such as he could not help, and though he might not work he must not starve. None must be abused for their natural infirmities; even the deformed child in the family must have its child's part. Calvin takes the rule where he takes most of the ceremonial law. It is the same requirement laid on the sacrifices, of which none but perfect ones might be offered, so that Israel should know no victim could expiate sin but one possessing complete perfection; and the same is justly required of a priest, who cannot mediate between God and men unless he is free from every spot. From which it follows that a man of angelic purity was to be expected — and that the bodily imperfections enumerated here must be transferred to the soul, since if Christ's perfect cleanness did not wash away our impurity, no offering could come from us but what was foul and unsavoury.
20:
One word in the list is disputed and the dispute is worth following. Keil and Clarke both take gibben for a hunchback, and Clarke renders it gibbous; Gill reports that the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem paraphrase it quite differently, as one whose eyebrows lying cover his eyes, and that Jarchi understands it so, with other Jewish writers referring it to some deformity about the eyes, one authority defining the gibben as a man who has no eyebrows, or only one. Ellicott prefers that reading outright: the hair of the brows so thick and heavy and long that they meet and cover the eyes, interfering with sight and making the man unsightly. On how many such defects there are, the three counts do not agree. Clarke gives a hundred and twenty on Ainsworth's authority; Gill makes it a hundred and forty; Ellicott says the second-Temple authorities registered a hundred and forty-two.

Ellicott describes the machinery that number implies. A chamber stood in the Temple court where the Sanhedrin examined every priest before admitting him to the officiating staff, and at the end of each examination the men were divided in two: those pronounced disqualified put on black garments, wrapped themselves in black cloaks and went away in silence, while those declared fit put on white and joined their brethren, marking the day with a feast for their friends that opened with a benediction blessing God that no blemish had been found in the seed of Aaron. The rejected were not simply dismissed; they were set to work in the wood chamber, choosing timber sound enough for the altar, since a worm-eaten piece could not be burnt on it. Clarke fills in the pagan parallels and then loses patience with his own church. Among the heathen the best-looking men were appointed to the priesthood: Metellus was refused it after losing an eye trying to save the Palladium from the burning temple of Vesta, since a priest defective in any member was held to be ominous, and at Elis the handsomest man was chosen to carry the sacred vessels. Formerly, Clarke says, the Church of England was cautious about admitting men with gross personal defects, and now we find them in her high places — why do our prelates ordain such?

What the blemished priest kept is as carefully stated as what he lost. Gill notes that such men were not impure in either a moral or a ceremonial sense, and so might eat of the sacrifices, which the impure might not — blemished persons, whether their blemishes were fixed or transient, might divide and eat but not offer — and that since they were priests, with no inheritance and no other way of getting a livelihood, provision was made so that they should not perish through defects laid on them by the providence of God. Wesley draws the distinction that governs the whole arrangement: God would show the great difference between natural infirmities sent upon a man by God and moral defilements which a man brings upon himself. Calvin finds in the same arrangement an admission against the system it belongs to. They were permitted the sacred meals and forbidden only to appear before God as mediators, and here the imperfection of the legal service betrays itself, since nothing could be found among men that could fully represent the truth; the defects of men made it necessary to separate two things that belong together, the honour and the burden, and by that separation Israel was admonished that another priest was promised them, in whom nothing would be wanting. He ends on the last verse, that Moses delivered these commands not to Aaron and his sons only but to all the people, so that the humblest of them might be a censor of the priests if in anything they fell short.
